20 pages · 11 models · 8 read twice

Benchmark · 11 models · 20 pages

Which model can read this page?

scroll ↓

One leaf of a 461-page Arabic scholarly edition.

Running head, body, a chapter heading, footnote anchors, the apparatus, a page number. Each is a different kind of thing.

A model has to know what each thing is.

Get one of them wrong and the app reads the running head aloud on every page.

An audit of 100 production pages found 365 defects. 275 were structural: running head in the body, page number in the body, footnotes merged. 79 were misreadings.

So we asked 11 models the same question.

The same 20 page images, the same instruction: give back the page as an ordered sequence of typed blocks, with the notes anchored where they belong.

…and scored them on 8 pages that were read twice, independently.

The reader is a model outside the ranked set. Every disagreement between its two readings was settled against the page image. No model in the ranking helped write the reference.

The answer.

Gemini 3.7 Flash scores highest. On 8 pages the evidence cannot separate it from Gemini 3.5 Flash, Claude Sonnet 5, Qwen 3.8 Max.

They span 1× in price. Pick on cost.

For the whole 461-page book.

Turn thinking off.

On Gemini 3.8 Flash, thinking tokens were 74% of what was billed. Off, the book costs $1.27 instead of $3.31 and accuracy holds at 99.75%.

The task

One leaf, five different kinds of thing. A model can read every character correctly and still return a page that is wrong, by putting them in the wrong bucket.

1
2
3
4
5
  1. 1
    Running head

    The section title, repeated on every leaf. Not body text — but it is the first line, so a flat-text parser calls it one.

  2. 2
    Page title

    This page's own heading. On this page it is the same word as the running head, which is why position alone cannot separate them.

  3. 3
    Body

    The prose. Everything else on the page is furniture, and any of it that lands here gets read aloud to the listener.

  4. 4
    Apparatus

    Numbered notes below the rule. Here note 1 contains a nested list in Greek, Latin and Arabic with two different digit systems.

  5. 5
    Page number

    Front matter carries its own series suffixed م; the body restarts with plain numerals. Two series, both incrementing by one.

The reason this matters downstream: whatever lands in body is what a read-aloud reader speaks. A running head filed as body is read out on every page; a page number filed as body is read out as a number in the middle of a sentence.

Which model reads this page correctly?

Every model answering the same request, scored against a fixed reference that no model in this table helped write.

Gemini 3.7 Flash has the highest score, and on 8 pages this evidence cannot distinguish it from Gemini 3.5 Flash, Claude Sonnet 5, Qwen 3.8 Max. Any of those four performs the task; the ordering between them is not a result, so choose on cost and on the specific failure each one still has.

And a limit worth stating. GPT 5.6 Terra, Kimi K3 score lower than all four, but the gap does not survive removing a single evaluation page for every member of the shortlist. On this evidence they are behind, not beaten.

How to read this. Scored on 8 pages, each read twice by a reader outside this field of arms, with every disagreement settled against the image. An arm must clear every gate (all 8 evaluation pages answered, body accuracy ≥ 0.95, footnote f1 ≥ 0.8, anchor f1 ≥ 0.8); among those that do, the score weights the prose first, then note text, anchor placement, block order, heading position, fields and markers. The band comes from resampling the 8 pages, and differences under 1 point are not evidence. Hover a cell for its denominator.

Which model?

Strictly these are model-plus-runner systems: the arms reached their answers by different routes (direct API, agent CLI), so a few tenths of a point may be the runner. The intervals at the top settle it.

Method

  • Same input everywhere. One 300 DPI page image per call. There is no OCR step and no text layer — the production pipeline is already a vision model, so this compares like with like.
  • One request. Every arm is asked for the same thing: one ordered sequence of typed blocks with inline footnote anchors, plus the running head, page number and the notes with their markers (prompts/P2_blocks.txt).
  • Accuracy comes from gold, and only from gold. 8 pages, picked on printed features before any scoring, each read twice by a reader outside this field of arms, with every disagreement settled against the image. Same reference for every arm; it does not move when the field changes. Denominators are printed on every cell.
  • Everything else is agreement, and says so. The 20-page figures compare an arm to the other arms. They are good at finding an outlier and structurally incapable of ranking a model, because the reference moves with the pool and a shared error passes unseen.
  • The decision rule was written before the scores were read — gates, then a weighted score over what the product depends on, then a bootstrap interval. Where two intervals overlap, no winner is claimed.
  • Cost is calibrated, not assumed. Production billed a measured $0.001881/page over 468 calls. Characters-per-token differs by output shape — 1.97 for Arabic prose, 2.79 for JSON, the latter measured directly from the API's own token counts.
  • Price provenance travels with every price: measured is real billing, list the vendor’s published rate, proxy a rate borrowed from a comparable model because none is published. Token volumes are measured for every arm either way; only the rate per token varies in how firmly it is known, and a subscription-routed run is priced at list with that fact recorded.

What this still cannot tell you. Gold is a careful independent reading, not a scholar's collation, so a misreading both readers shared would survive it. Each page was read once per arm, so run-to-run variation inside a model is not in the band.
